ety.text: From Middle English orchard, orcherd, from Old English orċeard, ortġeard, a compound of *ort (probably from Proto-Germanic *urtiz, a dissimilated variant of Proto-Germanic *wurt- (“wort (plant)”), later incorrectly associated with unrelated Latin hortus (“garden”)) + ġeard (see hortyard and yard, which ironically is etymologically linked with hortus). Cognate with Swedish örtagård (“herb garden”), Gothic 𐌰𐌿𐍂𐍄𐌹𐌲𐌰𐍂𐌳𐍃 (aurtigards, “orchard”), Old High German orzōn (“to cultivate a field”). Equivalent to wort + yard. More at root.

senses.d: A garden or an area of land for the cultivation of fruit or nut trees.
The trees themselves cultivated in such an area.

grp.label: land for cultivation of fruit or nut trees

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French vergier, from Old French vergier, from Vulgar Latin *virdiariu, syncopated form of Latin viridiārium, variant of viridārium, from viridis.

Borrowed from Old Occitan vergier, from Vulgar Latin *virdiāriu, from Latin viridiārium, variant of viridārium. Cognate with Ladino verdjel, Portuguese vergel, Galician verxel, Catalan verger, Occitan vergièr, French verger, and Italian verziere.

pt:pomar.gl: orchard (land for cultivation of fruit or nut trees)

ety.text: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *pomāre, from Latin pomārium, from pōmum (“fruit”). By surface analysis, pomo + -ar.

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin orchēstra, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀρχήστρα (orkhḗstra), from ὀρχέομαι (orkhéomai, “to dance”) + -τρᾰ (-tră, “a suffix used to form instrument nouns (pl.)”).

senses.d: A large group of musicians who play together on various instruments, usually including some from strings, woodwind, brass and/or percussion; the instruments played by such a group.
ex: The orchestra plays music for the dancers to dance to in the 19th century-styled dance hall.
Musicians play their instruments. I play the orchestra.

senses.d: A semicircular space in front of the stage used by the chorus in Ancient Greek and Hellenistic theatres.
The area in a theatre or concert hall where the musicians sit, immediately in front of and below the stage, sometimes (also) used by other performers.

ex: the jackhammering racket of the city softened and an orchestra of crickets trilled in unison
Nightfall also awakened the neighborhood orchestra of crickets.
